summary:
SmartFarmAI is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform developed by Team MSI to help farmers adapt to climate change, protect their crops, and use natural resources more efficiently.

Our solution combines NASA Earth observation and climate data, weather forecasts, artificial intelligence, drone-based monitoring, and precision irrigation into one integrated system.

Farmers can select their farm location on an interactive map, assess upcoming climate risks, identify potential threats to their crops using YOLO computer vision, and make informed irrigation decisions based on local soil and weather conditions.

SmartFarmAI aims to reduce unnecessary water consumption, prevent avoidable crop losses, improve farm productivity, and support long-term soil health. The platform also provides a foundation for future crop-rotation recommendations adapted to local environmental conditions.

Our mission is to transform space-based data into practical, accessible farming decisions — helping agriculture become more efficient, sustainable, and resilient to a changing climate.

An interactive 3D model shows how the whole system works, from satellite data to the farmer’s decision: https://blinchicfarm.netlify.app
details:
The problem

Agriculture accounts for about 72% of global freshwater withdrawals (UN SDG Report 2026). Up to 40% of global crop production is lost to pests and diseases (FAO estimate), and about 1.66 billion hectares of land are degraded by human activity (FAO). Irrigating “by eye” wastes water, diseases are often noticed late, ground sensors are too costly to cover a whole field, and a weather forecast knows nothing about the soil at one specific location.

How it works

Select a location. The user clicks any point on a satellite or street map, or searches for a place.

Get soil moisture. The system retrieves root-zone moisture (0–100 cm) and surface moisture, with the source and date shown next to each value.

Determine soil type. Clay, sand and organic carbon content from SoilGrids give the soil class: sandy, sandy loam, loam or clay.

Compute the advice. Moisture is compared with the wilting point and field capacity for that soil. If the soil is drier than 50% of that range, the system calculates the deficit in millimetres, taking into account the crop’s root depth and the 48-hour rainfall forecast. The result is coloured green, yellow or red.

Check plant health. Photos or drone frames are analysed by a YOLO model, and the result is cross-checked against soil moisture to separate disease from drought.

Features

Soil moisture anywhere

The primary global source is NASA SMAP Level 4 (accessed through AppEEARS), which provides surface and root-zone moisture at about 9 km resolution with a three-year history. NASA POWER (MERRA-2 soil moisture) acts as a fallback while SMAP data loads, with Open-Meteo as a further fallback. A physical USB soil-moisture sensor, when connected, takes the highest priority, because it reflects conditions at the field in real time.

Irrigation advice

The deficit is calculated in millimetres from the soil’s wilting point and field capacity, the crop’s root depth and the expected rainfall. The recommendation shrinks when rain is forecast.

Crop-rotation advice

The module uses average summer moisture over three years and drought-tolerance scores per crop. Legumes receive a bonus and monoculture a penalty, producing a ranked suggestion for the next season.

Leaf disease detection

An Ultralytics YOLO model locates the lesion on the leaf and draws a bounding box around it, instead of assigning one label to the whole image. The farmer learns where the problem is, not only that there is one.

Model and training. The detector recognises around 30 classes of healthy and diseased leaves across several crops, including apple, pepper, maize, tomato, soybean and grape. Its training data includes PlantDoc (Singh et al., IIT Gandhinagar, CoDS-COMAD 2020; CC BY 4.0), a dataset of real-world, non-laboratory leaf images collected from the internet and annotated with bounding boxes. We combined it with other open datasets using our own merge script, which unifies class names across sources, removes unwanted classes, skips images left without labels, creates a validation split where a source has none, and flags classes with too few examples. The platform supports both detection and segmentation models.

Three ways to use it.

Single leaf photo. The user uploads a photo and gets the disease, a confidence score and the box. By default only confident detections are shown. An option reveals low-confidence results, clearly marked as less reliable.

Drone, camera or video. The user uploads several JPEG or PNG images from a drone or smartphone, or one video. Coordinates are read from the image metadata (GPS EXIF), and processing runs as a background job with progress shown.

Large images. For high-resolution frames, the image is cut into tiles so that small lesions are not lost when the frame is downscaled.

From detection to decision.

If the image has coordinates, the result is cross-checked with soil moisture for that point. A disease detected under normal moisture means drought is not the cause.

Each geotagged detection becomes a red marker on the map, so the affected spot can be found and inspected.

The assistant can explain the finding and suggest general prevention steps. Treatment products and doses are left to an agronomist.

Unknown conditions. The model recognises only the classes it was trained on. If an image shows a problem it cannot identify, the system does not guess a diagnosis. It tells the user that it could not recognise the condition, which does not mean the plant is healthy, and recommends having the plant inspected by an agronomist. Crops outside the training data (currently wheat and cucumber) are handled the same way, and a fine-tuning notebook for adding them is prepared.

Outbreak map

A photo with GPS coordinates becomes a red marker on the map, showing where on the field the problem was found.

Yield calculator

For each of 22 built-in crops, or a custom crop, the user enters area and current yield. The calculator shows how much harvest the system could preserve:

Potential yield = current yield ÷ (1 − L₁)

Yield after = potential yield × (1 − L₂), where L₂ = 5%

L₁ is the baseline loss rate without the system, set per crop and editable by the user. With an optional price per tonne, the result is also shown in money. The outputs are scenario estimates, not field-trial results.

AI farming assistant

A built-in chat assistant helps the farmer understand what the system shows and decide what to do about it. The field’s context (location, soil moisture, soil type, irrigation result, disease detections, drone log) is passed to it automatically, so the farmer does not have to describe the situation.

Explains. It puts results into plain language: why a status is red, what “moisture deficit” means, which data source was used and from what date.

Answers practical questions such as “When should I irrigate?”, “What is wrong with my field?”, “Where is the disease?” and “Which data were used?”.

Proposes strategic measures. Based on the field’s data, it suggests actions such as adjusting the irrigation schedule, choosing crops for the next season, planning inspections of flagged areas, and general prevention practices.

Adapts to the user. It offers four roles: agronomist, engineer, drone pilot and support.

Keeps the agronomist in charge. It does not prescribe chemical products or doses, and recommends that thresholds and treatments be verified by an agronomist.

Without an external language-model key, the assistant falls back to a built-in help module covering irrigation, SMAP data, diseases and crop rotation. Users can also add their own key.

Data sources

Source Data used Purpose

NASA SMAP L4 (via AppEEARS) Root-zone (0–100 cm) and surface moisture, 9 km cell Basis of irrigation and rotation advice; 3-year history

NASA POWER (MERRA-2) Modelled soil moisture Fallback while SMAP loads

Open-Meteo 48-hour rainfall forecast Reduces recommended irrigation volume

SoilGrids (ISRIC) Clay, sand, organic carbon Soil type classification

USB soil-moisture sensor Local soil moisture Highest-priority source when connected

PlantDoc and other open datasets Annotated leaf images Training of the disease model

Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap, Nominatim Map layers and place search Interactive map

Priority order: sensor reading first, then SMAP, then NASA POWER, then Open-Meteo.

Drone safety prototype

The system includes a bench prototype of an onboard safety controller for spraying drones. An ESP32 microcontroller reads roll and pitch from an MPU-6050 gyroscope and accelerometer many times per second. While the tilt is within 15°, a green LED is lit, the dashboard shows a green status and spraying is allowed. Above 15°, the ESP32 blocks spraying in hardware, the status turns red, and the server enforces the same rule as a second layer. Because the check runs on the board itself, it works even when the connection to the server is lost.

The ESP32 also creates its own protected Wi-Fi network, Drone_Control. A phone can connect without internet or a router and open 192.168.4.1 to see live tilt values and status. From the web dashboard, an operator can send commands (spray, photo, waypoint, waypoint mission). The drone polls the server for commands, so it works behind any Wi-Fi, and it replies “executed” or “rejected”. In the current prototype an LED stands in for the spray mechanism, and flight-controller behaviour is simulated. Real waypoint flight would be handled by an ArduPilot or PX4 flight controller.

Technology

Python and FastAPI back end; SQLite; Docker deployment; Ultralytics YOLO; Leaflet map front end in HTML and JavaScript served by the same server as the calculations; ESP32 and MPU-6050 hardware; Arduino-based soil-moisture sensor with a USB bridge for Windows, macOS and Linux.

Design principles

Transparent data. Every value shows its source and date.

Fail-safe sources. If one data source is unavailable, the system falls back to the next one.

Human in the loop. The agronomist verifies thresholds and chooses treatments. The assistant explains and suggests strategies but never prescribes doses.

Safety first. The spraying lock lives on the device, not only on the server.

Honest uncertainty. Low-confidence results are labelled, and unrecognised conditions are reported as such instead of being guessed.

Current limitations and next steps

Agronomic coefficients and moisture thresholds are approximate and must be validated by an agronomist.

SMAP provides one value per 9 km cell, not per individual field. The local sensor covers that gap.

The disease model does not yet cover wheat or cucumber. Its training images are mostly close-up, ground-level leaf photos, so accuracy on aerial drone imagery still has to be validated.

Detection is decision support, not a diagnosis. A confirmed finding needs a human check in the field.

The 15° tilt threshold is a conservative test value, to be refined in trials with a real sprayer. There is no physical drone yet, and real waypoint flight requires a flight controller.

Yield and water-saving figures are scenario estimates, not field results. Field trials are needed.
